paras: The lynching of Bill Parkman was the killing of a Black prisoner accused of burglary, taken with Henry Williams from his guards at Raleigh, Meriwether County, Georgia, in April 1888 by fifteen or twenty armed men. Parkman's beaten and burned body was found the next morning near Cane Creek. Williams, at first reported lynched too, turned up alive days later.

On a Monday night in mid-April, a trunk holding tobacco, a pistol and $25 or $30 was taken from a Mr. Bryan's house at Raleigh. Officers Moreland and Jarrell arrested Williams and Parkman, both described as 'colored', as 'the supposed guilty parties'. Moreland deputised three men to guard them overnight, partly because Parkman was in 'very feeble health'.

While Moreland was at supper, the armed party took the prisoners from the guards; Moreland said two masked men held him at his door with shotguns, a claim the paper qualified with 'so he said'. The prisoners were taken toward Cane Creek, and Parkman's body was found in the swamp near the railroad crossing, his head and face beaten and his feet and legs badly burned.

Williams was discovered near Woodbury on a Wednesday and carried to the Greenville jail by about thirty-five armed Black men. Badly beaten, he said he knew every one of the sixteen men in the party. The paper expected 'startling developments', but no report of arrests, an inquest or a trial was found.

The only coverage found ran as two short paragraphs in the Savannah Morning News column of Georgia state news. The first told the story from the officer's side and called the killers 'the lynchers' without comment; the second corrected the report of Williams's death.

Williams said the party was fired into after killing Parkman and all fled but one man, whom he knocked down; a rumor held instead that he was left for dead and hid in neck-deep water most of the night.

reader.title: Lynching of Bill Parkman
bases: Two Black prisoners accused of burglary were taken from their guards by an armed party and one, Parkman, was found dead, beaten and burned (A1, A2).

Parkman was found dead after a party of fifteen or twenty armed men (sixteen, by Williams's count) took him from the guards holding him on a burglary charge, and the paper called the men 'the lynchers' (A1, A2).
Both reports come from one paper's Georgia briefs column, the Savannah Morning News; the second adds Williams's own account but no independent paper was found (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News first report (officer's account)
accounts.gist: An armed party of fifteen or twenty took the prisoners from three deputised guards while Officer Moreland, by his own account held off by two masked gunmen, was at supper; Parkman was found dead and Williams was missing.

accounts.label: Henry Williams's account
accounts.gist: Williams said sixteen men took part, that after they killed Parkman the party was fired into and all ran but one, whom he knocked down.

accounts.label: Local rumor
accounts.gist: Another rumor held that the party left Williams for dead and he crawled into neck-deep water and stayed there nearly all night.

framing.detail: Short items in the 'Georgia' briefs column, between other state news; the paper names the killers 'the lynchers' and calls the victims 'the supposed guilty parties' and 'colored', with no editorial comment.

versions.value: Not seen since; unknown whether he escaped
